answers.text: A person makes every forward move, one step at a time. Meeting a gate does not move the mode by itself. The brief gives gates for shadow to both (7 days) and both to new_only (14 days plus Finance sign-off), but none for old_only to shadow, which is an open question. The rollout tool is the piece people use to move modes; its interface is not specified yet.

In shadow, customers pay the old engine's charges. The old engine charges and writes the ledger as today. The new engine reads the same usage events and writes its invoices to the shadow store. The shadow store is a separate store. The ledger is the system of record, and the new engine never writes it in shadow.

Checked: the nightly job compares each customer's invoice totals from the two engines. A mismatch is a total that differs by more than one cent. A day counts toward the 7-day gate only if its mismatch rate is under 0.1 percent and at least 5,000 invoices are compared, and the 7 days must be consecutive. Unknown: what the job writes to comparison_results. Also unknown: whether the 5,000-invoice minimum is per day or across the 7 days. The brief does not say, so I have not guessed.

In both, the new engine is the source of charging. It charges and writes the ledger. The old engine computes every invoice into the shadow store without charging. So each customer is charged once, by the new engine. The brief forbids any double charge.

Checked: the billing monitor watches the new engine's charge failure rate in both and new_only. If the rate is above 2 percent over any 10-minute window, it starts a rollback on its own. New-engine errors in shadow never trigger it. Unknown: whether it changes billing_mode directly or starts the rollout tool. The brief does not say.

pause_charging stops the new engine from charging. resume_charging restarts charging under the old engine, so that no due charge is dropped. Catch_up is the old engine reprocessing usage events it skipped in new_only, read from the usage event log. It is not needed from both, where the old engine kept computing. Unknown: how usage that arrives during the pause is handled, and how a due charge is kept safe during the switch. The brief does not say.
Reconcile checks results customer by customer and billing period by billing period. The brief does not say what the rollback record holds or who reads it. I have not guessed; it is an open question.

Retry: each step must be safe to run again, because the brief forbids double charges. A failed step is retried. The brief gives no retry limit, which is an open question. Skipped steps: from shadow, pause, switch, reconcile and resume are skipped, because the new engine never charged or wrote the ledger and the old engine has charged all along. From both, catch_up is skipped, because the old engine kept computing. From new_only, all steps run.

Gates reset means the rollout returns to shadow and the 7-day count starts at zero. The path back to new_only runs through both, so the 14-day count in both starts over too. Finance sign-off is needed again, because the brief resets all gates and Finance sign-off is one of them. The 35-day clock is counted from entering new_only. The usage event log keeps events for 35 days and catch_up reads them from it, so the first skipped events age out on day 35, which matches the no-way-back rule.

answers.text: billing_mode keeps its value from before the rollback while the steps run, and changes to old_only only when the whole rollback finishes, after resume_charging. Reason: the flag should describe a finished state, and the brief defines only four mode values, so no extra value is added. Whether the flag should show an in-progress value is left open in the file.

Checked: in both, the old engine computes every invoice into the shadow store without charging, so its invoices are ready. The brief does not say how switch_to_old makes it charge and write the ledger again (a config change, the rollout tool, or something else). I have not guessed. It is an open question in the file.

reconcile only checks and reports wrong customers or billing periods. It does not charge, refund or change ledger rows itself. Reason: an automatic fix could itself cause a double charge, which the brief forbids. Who fixes a finding, and whether a finding blocks resume_charging, is not known and is an open question.
The brief does not say what makes a mismatch resolved or who resolves it. I have not guessed. It is an open question in the file.

Checked: the brief says on-call can start a rollback by hand at any time within the 35-day limit. It does not say how, and does not say the rollout tool is the route. Unknown, and an open question. Decided for the running case: a second start does not begin a second rollback, because two rollbacks at once could interleave steps and charge someone twice.

Checked: when the rollback is from both or new_only, no engine charges from pause_charging until switch_to_old finishes, because pause_charging stops the new engine and the old engine only charges after switch_to_old. The brief says no due charge may be dropped, but it does not say when the waiting charges are made. Unknown: whether anyone is alerted, and the retry limit, which was already an open question. Both are listed as open questions.

answers.text: The list is right and the note is wrong. From shadow all five steps are skipped: pause_charging, switch_to_old, reconcile and resume_charging because the new engine never charged or wrote the ledger and the old engine always charged, and catch_up because the old engine kept computing. So a rollback from shadow runs no steps. It sets billing_mode to old_only at once and resets the gates. The notes now say no steps run from shadow.

Nothing moves new_only to decommissioned automatically. The brief says the old engine 'may be' decommissioned after 35 days, so a person decides. The diagram arrow is labelled as a person's decision. The brief does not say what decommissioning involves, so the file does not define it and it is listed as an open question.

The brief says a second start does not begin another rollback, which guards against a repeat start by the monitor or on-call. The brief does not say whether a forward move is blocked during a rollback. I decided it is refused, because billing_mode still shows both or new_only during the steps and a forward move could run alongside them. The rule is in the Forward moves section. The rollback record's in-progress fact is what the guard checks.

The rollback record holds the in-progress fact and the current step. The brief says the record shows a rollback is in progress, but not how a retry knows where it stopped. Recording the current step is the smallest way to meet the retry rule. Its other contents are not given by the brief and are left open.

The brief does not say whether a single failed new-engine charge in both is retried. It counts toward the charge failure rate. The brief does require that no due charge is dropped, and resume_charging restarts charging under the old engine. So a failed charge that is still due must be made after the rollback, but the brief does not say how the old engine finds it. I have not guessed. It is an open question in the file.

answers.text: The rollout tool checks the 7-day gate when a person starts shadow to both, and refuses the move unless the gate is met. A gate that a person checks by hand is not enforced, and the brief says a gate that is not met stops the move. The brief does not say which data the tool reads for this check, so that is listed as an open question. Changed the Forward moves step 2 text to say this.

Yes. Starting a rollback writes the rollback record first, with the current step set to pause_charging, because the brief says the record is written when a rollback starts. The five steps then run in the listed order, and the current step is updated in the record as each begins. The brief does not say what runs them (the rollout tool, the monitor, or another process), so that is an open question.

This is what the document intends. In both, the new engine keeps charging the other customers after one charge fails. Customers are not charged by either engine only from pause_charging until switch_to_old ends. The 2 percent over any 10-minute window is the only automatic stop the brief names. On-call can stop charging earlier by starting a rollback at any time. The brief does not say whether a single failed charge is retried. Added one sentence to the failure table row for a failed charge in both.

The brief says reconcile checks results customer by customer and billing period by billing period. It does not name the two sources it compares. In both, the new engine's invoices are in the ledger and the old engine's are in the shadow store, but the brief does not say reconcile reads them. I have not guessed. Added as an open question.

In the file's logic, a rollback cannot finish while a step is failing. billing_mode changes only after resume_charging, and each failed step is retried. So a stuck step keeps the rollback open and the mode at its old value, and the failure table now says so. The brief gives no retry limit, does not say whether a reconcile finding blocks resume_charging, and does not say what the person running it sees. These are open questions.

The brief limits when a rollback from new_only must start (within 35 days). It does not limit when it must finish. It also does not say whether catch_up must finish before day 35, when the first skipped events expire from the usage event log. A rollback started on day 34 may not be able to finish. I have not guessed. Added as an open question.

teachbacks.text:
1. Starting point. Today the old engine does all billing. Billing workers read usage events from the usage event log (kept 35 days), compute invoices, write them to the billing ledger (the system of record) and charge customers through the payment provider. One global flag, `billing_mode`, held by the config service, says which mode we are in: `old_only`, `shadow`, `both` or `new_only`, in that order.

2. Moving forward from `old_only` to `shadow`. A person uses the rollout tool to start this move. The document sets no gate for it. The new engine starts reading the same usage events and writing its invoices to the shadow store (not the ledger). `billing_mode` becomes `shadow`. The old engine still charges and writes the ledger. The new engine never charges and never writes the ledger.

3. Running in `shadow`. Each night the nightly comparison job compares the two engines' invoices customer by customer and writes results to `comparison_results`. A customer whose two totals differ by more than one cent is a mismatch, and the share of mismatches is the mismatch rate. New-engine errors are recorded but never start a rollback.

4. Moving from `shadow` to `both`. A person asks the rollout tool to move. The tool checks the gate: 7 consecutive days with mismatch rate under 0.1 percent and at least 5,000 invoices compared. If the gate is not met, the tool refuses and `billing_mode` stays `shadow`. Meeting the gate never moves the mode by itself. Forward moves are also refused while a rollback is in progress. If the gate is met and the person proceeds, the new engine starts charging and writing the ledger, and `billing_mode` becomes `both`. Each customer is charged once, by the new engine. The old engine keeps computing invoices into the shadow store without charging, and the comparison continues.

5. Running in `both`. The billing monitor watches the new engine's charge failure rate. One failed charge counts toward the rate, and the new engine keeps charging other customers. If the rate is above 2 percent over any 10-minute window, the monitor starts a rollback (see step 8). Unresolved mismatches block the next move.

6. Moving from `both` to `new_only`. A person asks the rollout tool. Gate: 14 days in `both` with no unresolved mismatches, plus Finance sign-off. If it is not met, the move is refused. If it is met, the old engine stops computing and `billing_mode` becomes `new_only`. The 35-day clock starts. The monitor keeps watching the failure rate here too.

7. After 35 days in `new_only` with no rollback. A person may decide to decommission the old engine. Nothing does it automatically. From day 35 there is no way back, because the usage event log no longer holds the events that catch up would need.

8. Starting a rollback. On-call can start one by hand at any time (from `new_only` it must start within the 35 days). The monitor starts one automatically in `both` or `new_only` on the 2 percent trigger. A second start while one is running does nothing. Starting writes the rollback record first, with current step `pause_charging`. The record shows a rollback is in progress and holds the current step. From now on forward moves are refused. `billing_mode` keeps showing the old value during the whole rollback.

9. Rollback from `shadow`. The record is written, no steps run, `billing_mode` is set to `old_only` at once, and gates reset.

10. Rollback from `both` or `new_only`: steps run in order, and the current step in the record is updated as each begins. Every step is safe to rerun, and a failed step is retried, so a retry cannot double-charge. Rules throughout: no customer charged twice for a billing period, no due charge dropped.
   a. `pause_charging` stops the new engine charging.
   b. `switch_to_old` makes the old engine charge and write the ledger again.
   c. `catch_up` runs only from `new_only`. The old engine reprocesses the usage events it skipped, read from the usage event log.
   d. `reconcile` checks customer by customer and billing period by billing period and reports each wrong one. It does not charge, refund or change ledger rows.
   e. `resume_charging` restarts charging under the old engine so no due charge is dropped.

11. Finishing a rollback. Only after `resume_charging` does `billing_mode` become `old_only`. All gates reset. The rollout must go through `shadow` again (7-day count restarts), then `both`, then `new_only` with the 14-day count and Finance sign-off again. A rollback cannot finish while a step keeps failing, since failed steps are retried.
